meta.title: Who really said "Excuse my dust"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuinely Parker: she sent "EXCUSE MY DUST!" to Vanity Fair as her own mock epitaph in June 1925 — but she didn't coin it, and it isn't on her grave.
meta.ogDescription: Confirmed in the June 1925 Vanity Fair scan: Parker borrowed a 1913 motorists' joke — and her Woodlawn headstone quotes a different poem.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Genuinely hers, and locatable to the page: Parker submitted “EXCUSE MY DUST!” as her own mock epitaph to Vanity Fair for June 1925, in a feature called “A Group of Artists Write Their Own Epitaphs.” Two caveats that matter: she did not coin the phrase — it was already a joke sign on the back of automobiles by 1913 — and it is not the inscription on her grave.

source.heading: The source, in full

docMeta.dd: A Group of Artists Write Their Own Epitaphs
Vanity Fair, vol. 24, no. 4 — June 1925, Condé Nast, New York
A self-composed mock epitaph, printed as a drawing of a headstone

source.excerpt:
Some Well-Known People Seize the Coveted Opportunity of Saying the Last Word

A number of artists, desiring to be saved from the ordinary run of tombstone literature, have here set down their epitaphs. This second batch of epitaphs, like those published in Vanity Fair in its October issue, certainly have the invaluable “personal touch”…

CI-GIT
Dorothy Parker
“EXCUSE MY DUST!”
trail: The primary issue, read directly. The Internet Archive’s scan of Vanity Fair, vol. 24, no. 4 (June 1925) ↗ carries the feature “A Group of Artists Write Their Own Epitaphs,” its standfirst “Some Well-Known People Seize the Coveted Opportunity of Saying the Last Word,” and Parker’s drawn headstone reading CI-GIT / Dorothy Parker / “EXCUSE MY DUST!”

Specialist anchor. Quote Investigator ↗ records the citation as “1925 June, Vanity Fair, A Group of Artists Write Their Own Epitaphs, Start Page 50, Quote Page 51, Column 3… (Verified on microfilm),” and concludes: “in 1925 ‘Vanity Fair’ collected and published self-selected epitaphs from celebrities… Dorothy Parker chose the comical expression under examination. Yet, the phrase was already in circulation in the automotive world, and Parker had cleverly reimagined its meaning.” Wikiquote ↗ agrees, listing it in its sourced Quotes section as her proposed epitaph, quoted in Vanity Fair (June 1925).

The phrase predates her. QI’s earliest citations are both from 1913 — the San Francisco Chronicle of 10 June and the humour magazine Judge of 13 December — and the phrase was familiar enough by 1920 to title a Wallace Reid racing picture for Famous Players–Lasky ↗, a print of which survives at the Library of Congress. So the words are Parker’s choice, not her invention.

What is on the stone. The headstone unveiled at Woodlawn Cemetery in the Bronx on 23 August 2021 does not carry this line; the reported inscription ↗ is the closing stanza of “Epitaph for a Darling Lady,” which appears in Enough Rope (Boni & Liveright, 1926) ↗ as: “Leave for her a red young rose, / Go your way, and save your pity; / She is happy, for she knows / That her dust is very pretty.”
source.excerptNote: Parker’s entry is not a sentence in an essay — it is a small drawing of a headstone, one of roughly two dozen across the spread, alongside George Gershwin, W. C. Fields and the Four Marx Brothers. Ci-gît is the French formula for “here lies”: exactly the “tombstone literature” the feature set out to mock. Text as read in the Internet Archive’s scan of the issue, whose transcription does not reproduce accents.

source.rightsNote: Parker’s epitaph version reached print in Vanity Fair for June 1925 — the phrase itself was already in print by 1913 — comfortably before the 1931 cutoff that governs US public-domain status, and the whole issue is freely readable at the Internet Archive ↗. Parker wrote in English, so no translation rights arise — though this covers only the three words as printed in 1925, not her later books, which are a separate question.

author.name: Dorothy Parker
author.heading: Who was Dorothy Parker?
author.bio: Born in Long Branch, New Jersey on 22 August 1893, Parker wrote her way from a job at Vogue into the drama-critic’s chair at Vanity Fair, and became the sharpest voice at the Algonquin Round Table — the lunch circle of New York writers whose wisecracks were syndicated across the country in the 1920s. Her verse collection Enough Rope (1926) was a bestseller, and she later wrote for Hollywood before being blacklisted for her politics. She died in New York on 7 June 1967, leaving her literary estate to Martin Luther King Jr. — a bequest that, after his assassination, passed to the NAACP and eventually put her ashes in a memorial garden in Baltimore.

cite.sourceCitation: "A Group of Artists Write Their Own Epitaphs." Vanity Fair 24, no. 4 (June 1925): 50–51. Dorothy Parker's entry appears on page 51, column 3 (citation as recorded by Quote Investigator, verified on microfilm); wording independently confirmed in the Internet Archive's scan of the issue.
cite.pageCitation: Quotle.info. “Who really said ‘Excuse my dust’?” Last verified 17 Aug 2026.

copyAttribution: "Excuse my dust!" — Dorothy Parker, submitted as her own mock epitaph to Vanity Fair, June 1925 ("A Group of Artists Write Their Own Epitaphs," pages 50–51; Parker's entry on page 51). Parker did not coin the phrase: it circulated from 1913 as a joke sign on the backs of automobiles. Nor is it the inscription on her grave — the headstone unveiled at Woodlawn Cemetery, the Bronx, on 23 August 2021 carries the closing stanza of her poem "Epitaph for a Darling Lady." Verified by Quotle.info.

misattribution.heading: The author is right. Almost everything around it is wrong.
misattribution.intro: This one survives verification cleanly, so the failures are not about who — they are about what the words are and where they ended up. Three recurring errors:

items.who: Parker, credited with inventing the phrase
items.why: It was already motoring slang. Quote Investigator ↗ documents “Excuse my dust” in 1913 — a 10 June item in the San Francisco Chronicle and a 13 December cartoon in Judge — and it was the title of a 1920 Wallace Reid automobile-racing film ↗. QI’s verdict is that “the phrase was already in circulation in the automotive world, and Parker had cleverly reimagined its meaning.”

items.who: Presented as the inscription on her tombstone
items.why: Her headstone at Woodlawn Cemetery in the Bronx, unveiled on 23 August 2021, carries the closing stanza of her poem “Epitaph for a Darling Lady” ↗ instead. The phrase did appear on the 1988 NAACP memorial plaque in Baltimore, but in reported form — “For her epitaph she suggested, ‘Excuse my dust’” ↗ — not as the epitaph itself.

items.who: Confused with “Here lies the body of Dorothy Parker. Thank God!”
items.why: That is her other self-composed epitaph, from the earlier Vanity Fair round in October 1924 (pp. 42–43), and Quote Investigator treats the two separately ↗. The pair are routinely quoted as one line, or swapped for each other.

misattribution.truthLine: The attribution holds and the wording is exact: Parker sent these three words to Vanity Fair for its June 1925 issue ↗ as a joke epitaph. Quote it as a printed magazine gag she wrote — not as a phrase she invented, and not as words on her stone.

context.heading: A motorists' apology, parked on a tombstone
lead: Vanity Fair ran the gag twice. In its October 1924 issue it invited well-known people to compose their own gravestones, and the June 1925 spread introduces itself as the sequel: “A number of artists, desiring to be saved from the ordinary run of tombstone literature, have here set down their epitaphs. This second batch of epitaphs, like those published in Vanity Fair in its October issue, certainly have the invaluable ‘personal touch’…” Parker had supplied one for the first round too — “Here lies the body of Dorothy Parker. Thank God!” ↗ — so the three words everyone remembers were, strictly speaking, her second attempt.

The joke depends on something a 1925 reader would have caught instantly and a modern reader usually misses. “Excuse my dust” was motoring slang: a mock-apology hung on the back of a fast car for the cloud it threw at everyone behind it. Quote Investigator ↗ traces it to 1913 — a 10 June item in the San Francisco Chronicle and a 13 December cartoon in the humour magazine Judge — and by 1920 it was good enough to title a Wallace Reid racing picture ↗. Parker’s contribution was not the phrase but the swerve: she took a boast about speed and made it an apology from the grave. Her entry is even drawn as a headstone, headed CI-GIT — French for “here lies” — which is exactly the pompous “tombstone literature” the feature set out to mock.
context.detailsSummary: What is actually carved on her grave
detailsBody: Parker died in New York on 7 June 1967. Her ashes went unclaimed for years, and in 1988 they were interred in a memorial garden at the NAACP’s Baltimore headquarters. The plaque there did carry the phrase — but as a report, not as an epitaph: “For her epitaph she suggested, ‘Excuse my dust’” ↗, set inside a longer dedication to her as a defender of human and civil rights.

In August 2020 the urn was quietly moved to Woodlawn Cemetery in the Bronx, where her family had always intended her to lie, and on 23 August 2021 a headstone was unveiled. It does not say “Excuse my dust.” The family chose the closing stanza of her poem “Epitaph for a Darling Lady,” collected in Enough Rope (1926) ↗:
“Leave for her a red young rose, / Go your way, and save your pity; / She is happy, for she knows / That her dust is very pretty.”
Which is its own small joke on the researcher: the stone that turned down her famous dust line ends on the word dust anyway.
context.pull: She took a boast about how fast you were going and turned it into an apology for what you'd become.

isPartOf.name: Vanity Fair, vol. 24, no. 4 (June 1925): "A Group of Artists Write Their Own Epitaphs"

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator documents that Dorothy Parker submitted "EXCUSE MY DUST!" as her own epitaph to Vanity Fair, June 1925, citing "A Group of Artists Write Their Own Epitaphs," start page 50, quote page 51, column 3, verified on microfilm; and that the phrase was already circulating in the automotive world, with 1913 citations from the San Francisco Chronicle (10 June) and Judge (13 December).

Quote Investigator documents "Here lies the body of Dorothy Parker. Thank God!" as a separate epitaph Parker submitted to Vanity Fair for its October 1924 issue (start page 42, quote page 43), notes the words were never used on her gravestone, and references "Excuse My Dust" as her contribution to the June 1925 follow-up collection.

Wikiquote lists "Excuse my dust." in its sourced Quotes section for Dorothy Parker with the note "Her proposed epitaph for herself, quoted in Vanity Fair (June 1925)" — not under Misattributed or Disputed.

The Internet Archive's scan of Vanity Fair, volume 24, issue 4 (June 1925) contains the feature "A Group of Artists Write Their Own Epitaphs," its standfirst "Some Well-Known People Seize the Coveted Opportunity of Saying the Last Word," the introductory note about a "second batch of epitaphs, like those published in Vanity Fair in its October issue," and Parker's drawn headstone reading CI-GIT / Dorothy Parker / "EXCUSE MY DUST!" (confirmed by downloading and searching the item's full-text OCR).

The Internet Archive's scan of Vanity Fair, October 1924 (vol. 23, no. 2) lists "A Group of Artists Write Their Own Epitaphs . 42 and 43" in its contents, carries the same standfirst, and shows Parker's entry on page 43 reading "Dorothy Parker / THANK GOD!" (confirmed via the item's full-text OCR).

Wikipedia gives Dorothy Parker's birth as 22 August 1893 in Long Branch, New Jersey and her death as 7 June 1967 in New York City; records her roles at Vogue, Vanity Fair and The New Yorker; notes her ashes went unclaimed until 1988 when they were claimed by the NAACP; transcribes the Baltimore memorial plaque including "For her epitaph she suggested, 'Excuse my dust'"; and records the August 2020 exhumation and reburial at Woodlawn Cemetery in the Bronx.

Baltimore Fishbowl reports that Dorothy Parker's Woodlawn Cemetery headstone was revealed on Monday, 23 August 2021, inscribed with lines from her poem "Epitaph For A Darling Lady" — "Leave for her a red young rose / Go your way and save your pity / She is happy for she knows / That her dust is very pretty" — rather than "Excuse My Dust," which had marked her former Baltimore grave; it also notes she left her estate to Martin Luther King Jr. and that the reinterment occurred in August 2020.
The Dorothy Parker Society reports the Woodlawn Cemetery gravestone was unveiled on 23 August 2021 and that the family chose lines from "Epitaph for a Darling Lady" rather than "Excuse my dust."

Project Gutenberg's text of Dorothy Parker's Enough Rope: Poems (Boni & Liveright, 1926) contains the poem "Epitaph for a Darling Lady," whose final stanza reads: "Leave for her a red young rose, / Go your way, and save your pity; / She is happy, for she knows / That her dust is very pretty."

Wikipedia records Excuse My Dust (1920) as a surviving American silent automobile-racing film starring Wallace Reid, produced by Famous Players–Lasky and distributed by Paramount, preserved in the Library of Congress.

The Wheeler Centre's fact-check states that Parker joked during her lifetime that "Excuse my dust" would make the perfect epitaph, and that these words appear above her resting place but are not the only words marking her memorial, which also reads "Here lie the ashes of Dorothy Parker (1893-1967) Humorist, writer, critic, defender of human and civil rights..."
